subject: English
passage: Carbon found in the tissues of young Douglas fir seedlings is an example of a transferred nutrient—that is, a nutrient that originated in one plant and was later taken up by another. The carbon reached the seedlings indirectly from mature paper birch trees growing nearby. The birches had produced it through photosynthesis in their leaves, from which it traveled downward into their roots. Nitrogen found in the same seedlings is also transferred in origin and reached them through the same underground fungal network. But in this case, the original source was a patch of alders, nitrogen-fixing trees that host bacteria in their root nodules, as researchers Leila Sow and Nikolai Everett have documented.
prompt: The author makes which point about the underground fungal network?

choices.A: It has served as a medium through which nutrients from different tree species have reached Douglas fir seedlings.
choices.B: Its contribution of carbon to the seedlings roughly equals the collective contribution of nitrogen from other sources.
choices.C: It has received nutrients from mature trees and delivered nutrients back to them in return.
choices.D: It transferred carbon from birches and nitrogen from alders in approximately equal amounts.

explanation: Choice A is the best answer because it presents a point about the underground fungal network that is directly supported by the text. The text provides two examples of nutrients that reached Douglas fir seedlings: carbon from paper birches and nitrogen from alders. In both cases, the nutrients traveled through the same underground fungal network. Thus, the fungal network served as a medium, or intermediary, through which nutrients from different tree species reached the seedlings.
